title: Why Are We Using Machines to Study Our Inner Lives?
gist: Julie Sedivy's framing claim — that scientists are increasingly running experiments on chatbots rather than humans — is carried by the standfirst, while the surviving body text is a detailed account of how punishing human eye-tracking data collection was in her graduate years: hours of labor and dedicated lab time per participant, with runs discarded on calibration failure. The piece is cut off at Nautilus's paywall before the chatbot argument is developed.

insights.claim: Scientists are increasingly running psychology and language experiments on chatbots instead of on human participants.
insights.speaker: Julie Sedivy
insights.so_what: LLMs displacing human subjects means academic behavioral research becomes an API-spend line item — a quiet, recurring demand channel for model providers.
insights.quote: Increasingly scientists are testing chatbots rather than humans in experiments
insights.locator: Why Are We Using Machines to Study Our Inner Lives?

insights.claim: The author's framing question is skeptical rather than celebratory, treating the substitution of machines for humans in studies of inner life as something requiring justification.
insights.speaker: Julie Sedivy
insights.so_what: Signals a coming validity fight over LLM-as-participant results — a reputational risk for research built on synthetic subjects.
insights.locator: Why Are We Using Machines to Study Our Inner Lives?

themes.theme: Cost economics of human data collection

insights.claim: Collecting eye-tracking language data from a single human participant consumed several hours of labor plus dedicated lab time, making per-subject cost the dominant constraint on experimental scale.
insights.speaker: Julie Sedivy
insights.so_what: This is the cost baseline any synthetic-subject method is measured against — it explains the pull toward chatbots without needing a validity argument.
insights.quote: Data from a single person consumed several hours of labor and of dedicated lab time.
insights.locator: Data analysis was no less painful

insights.claim: Human subject data was routinely discarded when head-mounted eye-camera calibration degraded mid-session, adding an attrition tax on top of already high per-participant cost.
insights.speaker: Julie Sedivy
insights.so_what: Yield loss, not just unit cost, drives methodological substitution — synthetic participants have no calibration attrition.
insights.quote: A promising calibration might give way to twitchy tracking and the participant’s data would have to be thrown out
insights.locator: A promising calibration might give way

insights.claim: Legacy eye-tracking analysis required manually playing back video frame by frame and aligning gaze position with word onsets in the speech participants heard.
insights.speaker: Julie Sedivy
insights.so_what: Manual annotation pipelines like this are the highest-value targets for automation in behavioral research tooling.
insights.locator: It involved manually playing back video recordings

insights.claim: Eye tracking became established as a new method in language science specifically because it opened questions that had previously remained firmly shut, showing that instrumentation choice determines which questions a field can pose.
insights.speaker: Julie Sedivy
insights.so_what: The same logic implies chatbot-as-subject will reshape which questions get asked, not merely cut costs — a lens for judging which research tooling wins.
insights.locator: establishing eye tracking as an exciting new method
